accepted.question_text: Let G be a simple undirected graph with adjacency matrix A, and for vertices i and j let I be the set of all positive real numbers beta such that i and j are beta-subgraph equivalent, meaning [e^(beta A)]_ii = [e^(beta A)]_jj. Theorem 2.5 shows that if I has an accumulation point then i and j are cospectral, in the sense that [A^r]_ii = [A^r]_jj for every integer r >= 0, and I is all of R_+. Determine whether some weaker finiteness hypothesis already forces the same conclusion: for example, if I is finite, or if M = |I| satisfies a suitable condition, must i and j already be cospectral?
accepted.context_brief: Finite sets of beta-subgraph equivalence values

evidence.quote: Definition 2.2. Two vertices i, j of G are cospectral if for every integer r >= 0, [A^r]_ii = [A^r]_jj.

Theorem 2.5. Given two vertices i, j of G, let I be the set of all beta > 0 such that i and j are beta-subgraph equivalent. If there is a beta0 in I which is an accumulation point for a sequence in I, then i and j are cospectral and I is necessarily all of R+.
It is natural to ask if this result can be improved. For example, is it still true if I is finite? Is there any condition on M = |I|, the cardinality of I, under which the result holds?

accepted.question_text: Let A be a non-diagonalizable n x n matrix whose entries are nonnegative algebraic numbers, viewed as the adjacency matrix of a weighted directed graph G, and let beta != 0 be an algebraic number. Determine whether the equality [e^(beta A)]_ii = [e^(beta A)]_jj for two vertices i and j necessarily implies that i and j are cospectral, meaning that [A^r]_ii = [A^r]_jj for every integer r >= 0, or else produce a counterexample.

evidence.quote: Definition 2.2. Two vertices i, j of G are cospectral if for every integer r >= 0, [A^r]_ii = [A^r]_jj.

Problem 1. Let A be a (non diagonalizable) n x n matrix, whose entries are all nonnegative algebraic numbers, regarded as the adjacency matrix of a weighted directed graph G. Let beta != 0 be an algebraic number. Prove or disprove the following statement: if for two vertices i, j we have [e^(beta A)]_ii = [e^(beta A)]_jj , then i and j are cospectral.

accepted.question_text: For subgraph centrality SC(i, beta) = [e^(beta A)]_ii, say that two vertices interlace at beta when SC(i, beta) = SC(j, beta). Given k in N, characterize the smallest graph or graphs that contain a pair of vertices with at least k interlacing values of subgraph centrality. Conversely, for a graph with n vertices, determine the largest possible number of interlacing values for a pair of vertices, decide whether there are graph classes for which the following bound is attained: if A has d distinct eigenvalues, then any two non-cospectral vertices have at most d - 1 interlacing values of subgraph centrality, and find simple constructions of graphs with many interlacing values.

evidence.quote: As mentioned in the Introduction, the subgraph centrality is defined as follows: SC(i, beta) = [e^(beta A)]_ii.
Definition 2.6. Let i, j be two non-cospectral vertices of a graph G. We say that i and j interlace at beta if SC(i, beta) = SC(j, beta); beta is an interlacing value.

Theorem 2.9. Let G be a (possibly weighted) undirected graph with adjacency matrix A, and denote by d the number of distinct eigenvalues of A. For any two non-cospectral vertices i, j there can be at most d - 1 interlacing values for the subgraph centrality.

Problem 2. Given k in N, characterize the smallest graph(s) with a pair of vertices that have at least k interlacing values of the subgraph centrality. Conversely, given a graph with n vertices, what is the largest number of possible interlacing values for a pair of its vertices? In particular, are there classes of graphs for which the bound d - 1 is attained?
A related, more informal problem is the following: is there a simple way to construct graphs with many interlacing values?

accepted.question_text: Theorem 2.9 states that if G is a weighted undirected graph with adjacency matrix A and d distinct eigenvalues, then any two non-cospectral vertices, meaning vertices i and j with [A^r]_ii != [A^r]_jj for some integer r >= 0, have at most d - 1 interlacing values for subgraph centrality. Determine whether the same bound remains valid for directed graphs, allowing positive edge weights.

evidence.quote: Definition 2.2. Two vertices i, j of G are cospectral if for every integer r >= 0, [A^r]_ii = [A^r]_jj.

Theorem 2.9. Let G be a (possibly weighted) undirected graph with adjacency matrix A, and denote by d the number of distinct eigenvalues of A. For any two non-cospectral vertices i, j there can be at most d - 1 interlacing values for the subgraph centrality.
Problem 3. Does Theorem 2.9 hold in the case of directed graphs? (Here we allow the graph to be weighted with positive weights.)

accepted.question_text: For a fixed pair of vertices in a graph G, compare interlacing for resolvent centrality RC(i, alpha) = [(I - alpha A)^(-1)]_ii, defined for alpha in (0, 1/rho(A)), and for exponential subgraph centrality SC(i, beta) = [e^(beta A)]_ii. Say that two vertices interlace when the corresponding centrality values are equal for some parameter value. Is it always true that the number of interlacing values for resolvent centrality is less than or equal to the number of interlacing values for subgraph centrality for that same vertex pair?

evidence.quote: As mentioned in the Introduction, the subgraph centrality is defined as follows: SC(i, beta) = [e^(beta A)]_ii.
Definition 2.6. Let i, j be two non-cospectral vertices of a graph G. We say that i and j interlace at beta if SC(i, beta) = SC(j, beta); beta is an interlacing value.

Let rho be the spectral radius of A and let alpha in (0, 1/rho). The resolvent centrality [15] (also called resolvent subgraph centrality) with parameter alpha is defined as follows: RC(i, alpha) = [(I - alphaA)^(-1)]_ii.

Problem 4. For a given pair of vertices of a graph G, prove or disprove the following statement: the number of interlacing values relative to resolvent centrality is always less than or equal to the number of interlacing values relative to subgraph centrality.
